name: Manjushri
summary: In Mahayana Buddhism, Manjushri is the bodhisattva of wisdom, usually shown with a flaming sword that cuts through confusion. He is linked to Mount Wutai in China and to the legend of Swayambhunath in Nepal.
about: Mahayana sutras present Manjushri as the bodhisattva of wisdom, often shown as a youth. In his raised hand he holds a flaming sword, which stands for wisdom that cuts through ignorance, and in many images he rides a blue lion. Several sutras say he is in fact a fully awakened Buddha who appears as a bodhisattva to help others. In the Vimalakirti Sutra he debates the nature of non-duality, and in the Lotus Sutra he helps the daughter of a naga king. Tibetan tradition, especially the Gelug school, honours him strongly, while Chinese Buddhists tell that Mount Wutai is his home. A Nepali legend says he drained the Kathmandu Valley lake. His many names include Wenshu in China and Monju in Japan.
kidSummary: Manjushri is the Buddhist bodhisattva of wisdom. He carries a flaming sword, but it only cuts away confusion, never hurts anyone. Stories say he rides a blue lion and once opened a mountain to drain a giant lake in Nepal.

story.title: A lake in a valley
story.text: In the Nepali legend, the Kathmandu Valley is a big lake. A shining lotus floats on it, and people can't reach it because of the water.

story.title: A journey from far away
story.text: The Swayambhu Purana says Manjushri came from the mountains of China to see the lotus, carrying his flaming sword of wisdom.

story.title: The sword opens a gap
story.text: Manjushri cut through the surrounding hills with his sword, and the water rushed out through the gap. The valley became dry land for people to live in.

story.title: A hill with a stupa
story.text: The lotus settled on the hill, and a stupa now stands there, called Swayambhunath. Many pilgrims visit it today.

teaches: Questions and debate help us learn
Cut through confusion with clear thinking

facts.text: A Korean legend says a boy washed King Sejo's back at Sangwonsa and eased his painful skin disease, then vanished; the king later had a statue made of the boy, Manjushri in disguise.
In an 8th-century Chinese painting by Wu Daozi, a ruyi sceptre replaces his usual sword; the scholar Berthold Laufer called it the first Chinese picture of a ruyi.
Yamantaka, whose name means 'terminator of Death', is a fierce form of Manjushri that is popular in the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism.
Pilgrims on Mount Wutai believe Manjushri may appear as an ordinary pilgrim, as a monk, or most often as strange five-coloured clouds.
In the Placing the Bowl Sutra, the Buddha is quoted as saying he reached Buddhahood through Manjushri's kindness, and that all past Buddhas were Manjushri's students.
The Swayambhunath stupa, also called the Monkey Temple for the monkeys on its hill, was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.
Chinese Buddhism honours a form called Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Bowl Manjushri, drawn with a thousand arms, each hand holding an alms bowl.
In one sutra he says he was once the teacher of Shakyamuni and now appears as his disciple, because a world should have only one main Buddha at a time.
Inscriptions of 782 and 792 show Java's Candi Sewu was first called the House of Manjushri; this royal Buddhist temple was built over 70 years before the nearby Hindu Prambanan.
In the Lotus Sutra, Manjushri leads the daughter of a naga king to awakening.
In some Vajrayana traditions his consort is the goddess Saraswati, and in Japan's Shingon school he is one of the Thirteen Buddhas that followers honour.
Qing histories say Nurhaci named the Manchu people after Manjushri, but historians still dispute where the name Manchu came from.
In Mongolian and Kalmyk folk tales, a giant called Manzashiri shapes the world from his body, and some think his name comes from Manjushri.
In Tibetan tradition the Arapacana mantra, built on a list of 42 letters, is believed to sharpen memory, debating and writing skills.
In Tibetan Buddhism he is sometimes shown in a trinity with Avalokiteshvara and Vajrapani, putting his wisdom beside their compassion and power.
In the Vimalakirti Sutra, Manjushri is the last bodhisattva to answer what non-duality is; the lay teacher Vimalakirti then replies with silence, a scene Chan and Zen teachers loved.
In that sutra Vimalakirti summons 32,000 huge lion thrones into his tiny room for Manjushri's visiting group, and the room does not grow at all.
Sutras say Manjushri is already a Buddha in a world called Constant Joy, beyond worlds as many as the sands of forty-two Ganges rivers, and will one day be a Buddha here, named Universally Seen.
The Avatamsaka Sutra places Manjushri on a clear, cold mountain in the north-east, which Chinese scholars matched to Mount Wutai; pilgrims were said to travel there from India by the 7th century.
The 9th-century Chan master Linji told students that those who seek Manjushri on Mount Wutai are wrong from the start; even so, the mountain stayed a major pilgrimage site.
The honorific 'Manjushri Emperor' was given to Qing rulers such as the Qianlong Emperor.

quiz.q: What does Manjushri's flaming sword stand for?
quiz.why: The sutras say the sword cuts through ignorance and confusion.

quiz.q: Which animal does Manjushri ride in many pictures?
quiz.why: The blue lion stands for taming the mind with wisdom.

quiz.q: According to the Nepal legend, what did Manjushri drain?
quiz.why: The Swayambhu Purana says he cut a gorge and drained the Kathmandu Valley lake.

quiz.q: Which sacred mountain in China is linked to Manjushri?
quiz.why: Mount Wutai is regarded as Manjushri's home in Chinese Buddhism.
